item.title: Sanitary board incumbents on track to keep seats over Turnacliff
item.description: Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens will win Richardson Bay Sanitary District board seats over challenger John Turnacliff in early Nov. 3 returns.
item.content:encoded:
Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens will win Richardson Bay Sanitary District board seats over challenger John Turnacliff in early Nov. 3 returns.

Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens will win new four-year terms on the Richardson Bay Sanitary District board, holding off challenger John Turnacliff in early returns from the Nov. 3 election.

Fitzgerald had votes on 50.1% of ballots counted, McIntosh on 48.8%, Walravens on 47.3% and Turnacliff on 19.5% in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 8:25 p.m. Nov. 3. Voters could choose up to three candidates, so the shares add up to more than 100%.

When those returns posted, 59,846 ballots had been counted countywide, about 34% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. The results are unofficial. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day could arrive as late as Nov. 10 and still be counted, and Marin County has until Dec. 3 to certify the results. The three winners will serve four-year terms through November 2030, joining sitting board members Mark Slater and Jeff Slavitz.

Keep election coverage free

The Ark doesn’t put its election coverage behind a paywall, so every voter in Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry can read it. A gift keeps it that way.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The district’s first contested election since 2018 came amid renewed debate over whether Marin’s sanitary districts should consolidate. The board voted unanimously July 21 to reject all seven findings and nine recommendations in a Marin civil grand jury report that urged special districts to explore consolidation. District officials argued that the report failed to account for existing joint operations or the financial risks of merging.

The incumbents largely defended the district’s operations during preelection interviews with The Ark. Fitzgerald, a Tiburon Fire Protection District captain and the son of Ark contract bookkeeper Marion Fitzgerald and her husband, Jim, emphasized preparing for staff turnover and maintaining fiscal discipline. McIntosh, the board president and co-founder of environmental-sensor company EnviroSmarts, stressed keeping sewer-service charges low and maintaining regional partnerships.

item.title: Saghezchi, Waterfield top Strawberry Rec race; Teese leads for third seat
item.description: Incumbents Sohrab Saghezchi and Sarah Waterfield will win Strawberry Recreation District board seats, and Chair Peter Teese leads for the third in early Nov. 3 returns.
item.content:encoded:
Incumbents Sohrab Saghezchi and Sarah Waterfield will win Strawberry Recreation District board seats, and Chair Peter Teese leads for the third in early Nov. 3 returns.

Incumbents Sohrab Saghezchi and Sarah Waterfield will win two of the three four-year seats on the Strawberry Recreation District board, and board Chair Peter Teese led challenger David Morgenthaler for the third in early Nov. 3 returns.

Saghezchi had votes on 44.8% of ballots counted, Waterfield on 44.4%, Teese on 39% and Morgenthaler on 31.2% in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 8:25 p.m. Nov. 3, when 59,846 ballots had been counted countywide, about 34% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters.

Waterfield did not publicly campaign or sit for an interview, and she has not said whether she would take the seat.

Keep election coverage free

The Ark doesn’t put its election coverage behind a paywall, so every voter in Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry can read it. A gift keeps it that way.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

Voters could choose up to three candidates, so the shares add to more than 100%. The results are unofficial. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day could arrive as late as Nov. 10 and still be counted, and Marin County has until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

In a separate race for the board’s one two-year seat, appointed incumbent Doug Twillman will win, with 68.3% of the vote to challenger Aliza Hawkins’ 31.7%.

The races marked a rare competitive election for a district that has long struggled to find residents willing to serve on its board.

Teese, a board member since December 2010, sought a fifth term. Saghezchi, a Mill Valley dentist whom county supervisors appointed in December 2022 after no one filed for the seat, sought election to it for the first time. Waterfield joined the board in December 2024 after running uncontested for a shortened two-year term.

Morgenthaler, a sales professional and musician, campaigned on expanding programs for teenagers and adding offerings such as foreign-language and music classes. Saghezchi emphasized transparency, fiscal responsibility and community involvement, while Teese said his top priority was completing the district’s planned playground.

item.title: Twillman set to keep Strawberry Rec two-year seat over Hawkins
item.description: Appointed incumbent Doug Twillman will win a two-year Strawberry Recreation District board seat, with 68.3% to Aliza Hawkins’ 31.7% in early, unofficial Nov. 3 returns.
item.content:encoded:
Appointed incumbent Doug Twillman will win a two-year Strawberry Recreation District board seat, with 68.3% to Aliza Hawkins’ 31.7% in early, unofficial Nov. 3 returns.

Appointed incumbent Doug Twillman will win a two-year seat on the Strawberry Recreation District board, taking more than two-thirds of the vote in early returns against challenger Aliza Hawkins, who sought the same seat by appointment last year.

Twillman had 68.3% of the vote to Hawkins’ 31.7% in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 8:25 p.m. Nov. 3, when 59,846 ballots had been counted countywide, about 34% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. The results are unofficial. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day could arrive as late as Nov. 10 and still be counted, and Marin County has until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

The candidates competed for a single two-year seat in a rare contested election for a district that has historically struggled to attract candidates. Their campaigns emphasized community engagement, financial oversight and the future of the district’s planned playground.

Keep election coverage free

The Ark doesn’t put its election coverage behind a paywall, so every voter in Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry can read it. A gift keeps it that way.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

Twillman joined the board in September 2025, when members selected him over Hawkins on a 3-1 vote to replace Cale Nichols, who had moved out of state. The election put that choice before voters.

A financial analyst and consultant with more than 30 years of experience, Twillman emphasized fiscal oversight and completing the playground at Strawberry Park. He serves on the board’s fundraising committee for the project and called for dependable cost estimates before construction commitments.

“The budget should be well understood so that we can hold the contractors accountable and the community can hold us accountable for a successful physical and fiscal outcome,” Twillman said during the campaign.

Hawkins, whose background includes marketing, advertising and counseling, focused on increasing participation in district programs and helping residents feel included and represented.

item.title: Paradise Cay’s Measure Z dredging tax set to pass with 84%
item.description: Paradise Cay’s Measure Z, extending the parcel tax that pays for canal dredging, had 84% support in early returns Nov. 3, above the two-thirds it needs.
item.content:encoded:
Paradise Cay’s Measure Z, extending the parcel tax that pays for canal dredging, had 84% support in early returns Nov. 3, above the two-thirds it needs.

Measure Z will pass, extending the special parcel tax that pays to dredge Paradise Cay’s canals and the two channels connecting the community to San Francisco Bay, with 84% of voters backing it in early returns Nov. 3. Vote counting was continuing.

As of 8:25 p.m., 16% of voters had opposed Measure Z. The measure needs approval from two-thirds of the votes cast to pass.

Measure Z sets the tax at $2,200 per lot a year in County Service Area No. 29 beginning July 1, 2027. The rate will rise automatically by 3% each year starting July 1, 2028, and the tax will expire June 30, 2037.

Keep election coverage free

The Ark doesn’t put its election coverage behind a paywall, so every voter in Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry can read it. A gift keeps it that way.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The service area estimates the measure will raise an average of about $272,800 a year for maintenance dredging in Paradise Cay’s principal waterways and the north and south entry channels. The tax applies to lots in the county-run district, which covers the Paradise Cay parcels with canal access rather than the whole neighborhood.

The district’s advisory board is planning its next dredging project for 2028 or 2029, said Eric Lyons, who chairs the board. The waterways were last dredged in 2020 and 2024, and the community typically needs dredging every four or five years, depending on how quickly sediment accumulates.

The 2024 project cost more than $1 million, including permits, planning, testing and other soft costs, Lyons said. The board’s forecast should cover dredging projects during the measure’s 10-year term, he said, though costs have been rising.

Measure Z will continue the existing parcel tax, which is scheduled to expire June 30, 2027. Paradise Cay voters approved the current tax, Measure O, in 2016 with 87.2% of the vote.

Reach Belvedere, Strawberry and public-safety reporter Tyler Callister at 415-944-4627.

Polls closed Nov. 3 at 8 p.m.

Live results for Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry. Marin posts new counts every few days until results are certified.

item.title: Elward leads Assembly race; billionaire tax trails statewide
item.description: Jackie Elward led Eric Lucan for the peninsula’s Assembly seat in early Nov. 3 returns, while Proposition 40’s billionaire tax trailed statewide and in Tiburon and Belvedere.
item.content:encoded:
Jackie Elward led Eric Lucan for the peninsula’s Assembly seat in early Nov. 3 returns, while Proposition 40’s billionaire tax trailed statewide and in Tiburon and Belvedere.

Rohnert Park Councilmember Jackie Elward led Marin Supervisor Eric Lucan for the Assembly seat representing the peninsula in election-night returns Nov. 3, while a one-time tax on billionaires trailed statewide and by even wider margins in Tiburon and Belvedere.

At the top of the ballot, Democrat Xavier Becerra will win the race for governor over Republican Steve Hilton, with a nearly 2-1 majority.

All results are unofficial and will change. The secretary of state’s 9:45 p.m. update counted ballots from 15,531 of the state’s 23,860 precincts, or 65.1%. Marin’s first report, posted at 8:25 p.m., counted 59,846 ballots, or 34.4% of the county’s 173,804 registered voters. The county is still counting late-arriving mail ballots, provisional ballots and ballots awaiting signature cures, and it won’t certify results until about a month after the election.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

On the peninsula, the county had counted ballots from 2,472 of Tiburon’s 7,553 registered voters, or 32.7%; 598 of Belvedere’s 1,618, or 37%; and 1,032 of Strawberry’s 3,081, or 33.5%. Peninsula figures are The Ark’s tallies of the precincts serving Belvedere, Strawberry and Tiburon, including unincorporated Tiburon areas such as Paradise Cay.

Results for the Tiburon Town Council, the Reed Union School District board and its Measure O bond, the Tamalpais Union High School District board, the Marin County Board of Education, the Richardson Bay Sanitary District, the Strawberry Recreation District and Paradise Cay’s Measure Z run in separate stories.

item.title: Ghaffary, Pasarell Tsai set to keep Reed seats as Godfrey, Antani battle for third
item.description: Mike Ghaffary and Shelby Pasarell Tsai will win seats on the Reed Union School District board of trustees, and Lina Godfrey led fellow challenger Krupa Antani by 16 votes for the third seat in early election-night returns.
item.content:encoded:
Mike Ghaffary and Shelby Pasarell Tsai will win seats on the Reed Union School District board of trustees, and Lina Godfrey led fellow challenger Krupa Antani by 16 votes for the third seat in early election-night returns.

Ghaffary led the four-person field with votes on 51.3% of the ballots counted in the race, or 1,792 votes, in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 8:25 p.m. Nov. 3, with 59,846 ballots counted countywide. Pasarell Tsai had votes on 49.1% of ballots, or 1,715 votes. Godfrey had votes on 36.3%, or 1,270, and Antani trailed the three leaders with votes on 35.9%, or 1,254.

Those results are unofficial. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive as late as Nov. 10 and still be counted, and Marin County has until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Keep election coverage free

The Ark doesn’t put its election coverage behind a paywall, so every voter in Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry can read it. A gift keeps it that way.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The top three finishers will win four-year terms that end in 2030.

“I’m very thankful that so many voters seem that they want to return me and that I’m thankful for the support,” Pasarell Tsai said.

Godfrey acknowledged that results were early and commended her fellow candidates for their campaigns, saying there were “four qualified candidates for these seats.”

“I’m hopeful that we had better turnout,” she said.

“I am grateful to all the students, parents, teachers and staff who work so hard in our school district every day. Thank you to our community for continuing to support our excellent Reed Union schools,” Ghaffary said.

“I think it’s important to let the process play out,” Antani said, adding that mail-in ballots have yet to be counted.

“Every vote matters, which is what we’re seeing in this race … so I think I’m in the mindset that we need to focus on letting this play out and getting the results in,” she said.

She said she was proud of the race and of the support for the race and for Measure O, adding that she would continue volunteering at Reed schools regardless of the results because she enjoys it.

item.title: Teacher-backed challengers ahead in Tam Union board race’s first count
item.description: Valerie Wynn, Brian Sutherland and Joy Scully Koo led the Tamalpais Union High School District board race in preliminary Nov. 3 returns, with President Cynthia Roenisch fifth.
item.content:encoded:
Valerie Wynn, Brian Sutherland and Joy Scully Koo led the Tamalpais Union High School District board race in preliminary Nov. 3 returns, with President Cynthia Roenisch fifth.

Three Mill Valley challengers endorsed by the district’s teachers union led the race for three Tamalpais Union High School District board seats in election-night returns, with board President Cynthia Roenisch running fifth.

Valerie Wynn, a retired district teacher, led the seven-candidate field with 13,990 votes, on 48.5% of ballots counted. Brian Sutherland, an appellate and constitutional lawyer, had 13,097, on 45.4% of ballots, and Joy Scully Koo, an engineer with an MBA, had 10,358, on 35.9%, according to the first preliminary results Marin County elections officials posted at 8:25 p.m. Nov. 3.

Former board President Leslie Harlander, a retired civil engineer, was fourth with 6,261 votes, on 21.7% of ballots, just ahead of Roenisch’s 6,152, on 21.3%, and more than 4,000 votes behind Koo. Spanish teacher Maria Sandoval had 4,078, on 14.1%, and Kevin Saavedra, who resigned from the board Oct. 9, had 3,520, on 12.2%.

Keep election coverage free

The Ark doesn’t put its election coverage behind a paywall, so every voter in Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry can read it. A gift keeps it that way.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The results are preliminary. That first update counted 59,846 ballots countywide, about 34% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. Results are not official until the county certifies them.

The district runs Redwood High School, the main public high school for Tiburon and Belvedere students, and Tamalpais High School, which serves Strawberry, along with Archie Williams High School in San Anselmo and two alternative schools. Board members are elected districtwide, so the race was on every peninsula ballot.

Taken together, peninsula voters put Sutherland first. In Tiburon’s precincts, he drew 1,063 votes to Wynn’s 1,006, and in Belvedere 261 to her 226. Strawberry voters put Wynn narrowly ahead, 419 to 406.

Koo was third in all three communities, with 706 votes in Tiburon, 176 in Belvedere and 310 in Strawberry. Harlander ran fourth in Tiburon with 639 votes, and Roenisch was fourth in Belvedere with 140 and in Strawberry with 234.

item.title: Ryan, Hornbrook and Defever will win Tiburon council seats
item.description: Jack Ryan, Chuck Hornbrook and Kathleen Defever will win the three Tiburon Town Council seats on the ballot after early election-night returns put them ahead of Faris Jafar and Alice Fredericks in the five-way race.
item.content:encoded:
Jack Ryan, Chuck Hornbrook and Kathleen Defever will win the three Tiburon Town Council seats on the ballot after early election-night returns put them ahead of Faris Jafar and Alice Fredericks in the five-way race.

Preliminary results as of 8:25 p.m. Nov. 3 showed Ryan leading the race with 1,177 votes, on 54.3% of ballots counted, followed by Hornbrook with 1,116 votes, on 51.5%, and Defever with 995 votes, on 45.9%. Jafar trailed with 747 votes, on 34.5%, and Fredericks had 642 votes, on 29.6%.

Because each voter could choose up to three candidates, the shares add up to more than 100%.

Keep election coverage free

The Ark doesn’t put its election coverage behind a paywall, so every voter in Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry can read it. A gift keeps it that way.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

Jafar and Fredericks both conceded election night.

The top three finishers will serve four-year terms until November 2030.

The results are unofficial. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day could arrive as late as Nov. 10 and still be counted, and Marin County has until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Ryan, the incumbent who first won a seat in a 2020 special election and a full term in 2022, said he was humbled by Tiburon voters’ choice in making him the leading vote-getter and looked forward to the new term.

“We’re going to have at least one new councilmember, and I’m excited to work with the new council in the new year,” he added.

Hornbrook, a Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission member who ran unsuccessfully in 2024, said he looked forward to addressing issues he heard on the campaign trail, estimating he knocked on some 900 doors.

He said he was excited to be “getting to work and helping deliver what the people of Tiburon want to get done.”

Defever, a Planning Commission member who ran unsuccessfully for the council in 2020 and 2021, said she had just seen the results when The Ark contacted her and was thrilled. The results were “something I’ve been looking forward to,” she said.

“I’m excited to have the voters’ support, and I cannot wait to get to work and get some of the issues I’ve heard about on the campaign trail addressed,” Defever said.

Jafar said he would help where he could.

item.title: Reed’s $115 million Measure O topping 55% bar in early returns
item.description: Reed Union School District’s $115 million Measure O bond had 58.5% support in early, unofficial returns Nov. 3, above the 55% it needs to pass.
item.content:encoded:
Reed Union School District’s $115 million Measure O bond had 58.5% support in early, unofficial returns Nov. 3, above the 55% it needs to pass.

Voters in the Reed Union School District were backing a $115 million bond to repair and upgrade the district’s three schools in early election-night returns.

Measure O received 58.5% support, or 1,886 votes, in the county’s first election-night count, released at 8:25 p.m. Nov. 3. That put it 3.5 percentage points above the 55% it needs to pass. Another 1,338 votes, or 41.5%, were against it, for 3,224 votes counted on the measure.

Results are preliminary. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive as late as Nov. 10 and still be counted, and Marin County has until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Keep election coverage free

The Ark doesn’t put its election coverage behind a paywall, so every voter in Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry can read it. A gift keeps it that way.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

Reed Union board President Shelby Pasarell Tsai, who was also on the ballot for reelection, said “early returns look good” and that she was feeling “hopefully optimistic for our school” district.

Pasarell Tsai said she was “really looking forward to community recognizing the importance of strong and vibrant schools, and it shows that our community really does value the schools.”

The tax would be levied on properties in the district, which includes Tiburon, Belvedere and east Corte Madera, beginning in fiscal year 2027-2028, when the district expects the rate to peak at $30 per $100,000 of assessed value. That works out to $300 a year for every $1 million of assessed value.

The district estimates the rate would average $26.63 per $100,000 over the life of the bonds, with the tax collected for the last time in fiscal 2060-2061. The levy would raise about $6.2 million a year, according to the ballot question, and the district’s tax rate statement estimates that repaying the full $115 million would cost $213 million in principal and interest.

No argument against Measure O was filed with the Marin County Elections Department.

item.title: Nemzer holds wide margin in Marin Board of Education’s Area 5
item.description: Tiburon resident Marilyn Nemzer led challenger Avery Lieberman in early, unofficial returns for the Marin County Board of Education’s Trustee Area 5 seat.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon resident Marilyn Nemzer led challenger Avery Lieberman in early, unofficial returns for the Marin County Board of Education’s Trustee Area 5 seat.

Tiburon resident Marilyn Nemzer led early returns in her bid for another four years on the Marin County Board of Education, ahead of a challenger backed by one of her board colleagues.

Nemzer had 71.6% of the vote, or 4,825 votes, to 28.4%, or 1,918 votes, for challenger and fellow Tiburon resident Avery Lieberman as of the county’s 8:25 p.m. Nov. 3 results report, when 59,846 ballots had been counted countywide, about 34% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters.

The Trustee Area 5 seat covers all of Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry as well as Corte Madera and Larkspur. The Reed Union School District lies entirely within its boundaries. The winner will serve a four-year term ending in November 2030.

Keep election coverage free

The Ark doesn’t put its election coverage behind a paywall, so every voter in Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry can read it. A gift keeps it that way.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The results are unofficial. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day could arrive as late as Nov. 10 and still be counted. Marin County has until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Nemzer said she was relieved and happy with the early results and that being elected is a special feeling.

“I just love being involved in what we do on the board, and I’m just really, really happy that it looks like I will have a chance to continue,” Nemzer said in a phone interview.

The Marin County Board of Education provides citizen oversight of educational programs and services run by the Marin County Office of Education. It works with the voter-elected county superintendent of schools to set county-office priorities.

Its duties include adopting or rejecting, but not modifying, the elected superintendent’s proposed budget; setting the superintendent’s salary; hearing appeals of student expulsions or denied interdistrict transfer requests; and maintaining positive relationships with the county’s 17 school districts.

Nemzer’s race became a proxy for existing tensions on the school board between her and board member Nancy McCarthy, who encouraged Lieberman to run and who has clashed repeatedly with her colleagues on the board.

item.title: Tiburon survey to shape smaller Cypress Hollow Park
item.description: Tiburon residents have until Nov. 9 to rank four playground concepts and pick equipment for a scaled-down rehabilitation of Cypress Hollow Park.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon residents have until Nov. 9 to rank four playground concepts and pick equipment for a scaled-down rehabilitation of Cypress Hollow Park.

Tiburon residents have until Nov. 9 to tell the town what playground equipment they want to see as part of a scaled-down rehabilitation of Cypress Hollow Park.

The online survey asks residents to rank four playground concepts that would fit in the existing playgrounds’ footprints and to pick the type of equipment, theme and color palette they prefer.

It also asks whether residents support removing certain trees to make room for a proposed accessible ramp connecting the upper and lower playgrounds and for new playground features.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: The four playground concepts in Tiburon’s Cypress Hollow Park survey would replace the equipment in the upper play area. Clockwise from top left: a 16-foot tree house with hammocks and a climbing net; a 14-foot modern tree house with a climbing wall; an 11-foot log structure with two slides and a rope-climbing tube; and a 12-foot main structure with fox, bird and butterfly climbers. item.title: Belvedere’s Lava House lots are listed for $30 million
item.description: The four vacant Belvedere Avenue lots where Jerry Ganz spent two decades fighting to build, known as the Lava House site, are for sale as one package for $30 million.
item.content:encoded:
The four vacant Belvedere Avenue lots where Jerry Ganz spent two decades fighting to build, known as the Lava House site, are for sale as one package for $30 million.

The four vacant Belvedere Avenue lots where the late seat-belt manufacturer Jerry Ganz spent two decades fighting to build, the site of the ruin known locally as the Lava House, are for sale as one package for $30 million.

The parcels at 399, 401, 415 and 419 Belvedere Ave. total about 2.75 acres above Richardson Bay, with views of the Golden Gate Bridge, the San Francisco skyline and Mount Tamalpais. The Sarkissian Bullock Team of Golden Gate Sotheby’s International Realty listed the land in mid-September and publicized it in an Oct. 29 news release.

The lots will not be sold separately, said Kevin Daniel Dwyer, the brokerage’s chief marketing officer. The site remains fenced, and showings are limited to “vetted, qualified buyers,” whom the agents walk through the property themselves, he said.

The listing lands as a new wave of artificial-intelligence wealth builds around the bay. San Francisco-based Anthropic filed Oct. 26 to go public, with a listing expected as soon as mid-November, and designer Jony Ive, whose AI-device startup OpenAI bought for $6.5 billion in 2025, paid $43.5 million last year for Belvedere’s Locksley Hall.

Dwyer pointed to the same money.

“The influx of wealth and the emerging affluent in the S.F. Bay Area from the AI and tech sectors presents a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for a qualified buyer,” he said in an email.

County records show 399, 401 and 415 are held by Belvedere 401 LLC, which took title in 2020 from the family’s 401 Belvedere Corp., and 419 by the Peggy Homestead Trust, a trust for Ganz’s daughter, Peggy. Stan Beainy, a longtime trustee for the family, died in December, and Ganz has also died, Dwyer said. The family is not available for comment, he said.

The lots are zoned R-15, Belvedere’s single-family district for parcels of at least 15,000 square feet. On any one lot, a home’s floor area may not exceed 33% of the lot or 4,850 square feet, whichever is less, though the Planning Commission can allow a larger house if it finds the lot has unusual features that lessen the impact of a bigger house, the extra space would not significantly block neighbors’ views or substantially reduce their privacy, and the house is appropriate in mass and bulk.

item.title: Strawberry swimmer completes 900-mile journey down California coast
item.description: Strawberry resident Catherine Breed finished a roughly 900-mile swim down the California coast Oct. 19, the first person to swim the state’s length, pending ratification.
item.content:encoded:
Strawberry resident Catherine Breed finished a roughly 900-mile swim down the California coast Oct. 19, the first person to swim the state’s length, pending ratification.

On her drive home to Marin from San Diego on Oct. 27, Strawberry resident Catherine Breed, a 33-year-old open-water swimmer, saw the California coastline from the road and took stock of her most recent odyssey.

“Oh my gosh,” Breed recalled thinking to herself. “I swam all of that.”

Breed the week before completed a roughly 900-mile journey called “Swim California,” navigating her way from the Oregon border all the way down to Mexico. She began July 1 and swam the coast in daily stages from a support sailboat over 111 days, 18 of them lost to weather and rest. When she finished her swim Oct. 19, Breed became the first person to swim the length of the Golden State, pending ratification by the World Open Water Swimming Association.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: The Strawberry resident swims Oct. 13 near Dana Point during Swim California, her roughly 900-mile swim down the California coast. (Emily Cameron via @catherine.breed / Instagram)

item.title: Golden Gate ferries back on schedule after four boats are sidelined
item.description: Golden Gate Ferry resumed regular Tiburon service Nov. 2 after an engine failure and three boats in dry dock put most weekday trips on buses for two weeks.
item.content:encoded:
Golden Gate Ferry resumed regular Tiburon service Nov. 2 after an engine failure and three boats in dry dock put most weekday trips on buses for two weeks.

Golden Gate Ferry is back on its regular schedule this week, Tiburon included, after an engine failure and three boats in dry dock put most weekday trips between Tiburon and San Francisco on buses for two weeks.

Regular service on every route resumed Nov. 2, the Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District said in a rider alert. District spokesperson Paolo Cosulich-Schwartz had said Oct. 30 that regular weekday Tiburon service would return once the ferry Golden Gate came back from dry dock.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Night shifts push Belvedere seawall work toward Nov. 13 finish
item.description: Crews shoring up Belvedere’s Beach Road seawall worked overnight to catch low tides; in-water work is now expected to wrap up about Nov. 13.
item.content:encoded:
Crews shoring up Belvedere’s Beach Road seawall worked overnight to catch low tides; in-water work is now expected to wrap up about Nov. 13.

Crews shoring up Belvedere’s Beach Road seawall worked overnight for much of the last two weeks of October to catch low tides, a push to finish in-water work the contractor now expects to wrap up about Nov. 13.

Tracy Rittenhouse, who lives on Beach Road near Peninsula Road, outside the stretch of homes the city emailed notifications to, said backup beeps from construction trucks woke her at 10 p.m. Oct. 19 and continued until 2 or 4 a.m. each night that week through Oct. 24. She said no one told her the night work was coming.

“They should have alerted everyone who lives on Beach Road,” she said. “Noise doesn’t stop at an address.”
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: A concrete pump truck and a ready-mix truck work along Beach Road in Belvedere the night of Oct. 30, as crews pour concrete to secure the seawall’s new steel sheet piles. The contractor expects to finish its in-water work about Nov. 13. (Joan Linn Bekins)

item.title: Tiburon, Mill Valley men turn trail runs into 25 years of friendship
item.description: TROT, an informal crew of Tiburon and Mill Valley runners, has bonded over 25 years of running together and six major trail runs since 2021.
item.content:encoded:
TROT, an informal crew of Tiburon and Mill Valley runners, has bonded over 25 years of running together and six major trail runs since 2021.

About 10 miles into running a stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail near Lake Tahoe with the informal crew of middle-aged Marin runners who call themselves TROT, Tiburon resident Park Allen felt an odd sensation under his foot.

Allen, 54, and the group of about 10 other men were deep in the woods, many miles from the car. He stopped to inspect his foot.

“I looked down and the entirety of the bottom of my shoe had come loose,” he said. “It was holding on by maybe a half an inch of glue.”

That 2023 story, the runners say, is one of dozens that have bonded TROT over 25 years of running together. The group, which varies in membership but centers on about 10 men from Tiburon and Mill Valley, has completed six major runs since 2021 — what Tiburon resident Bryan Breckenridge calls their informal “ultramarathons” — ranging from about 20 to 50 miles.

item.title: Del Mar Middle School joins new Marin middle school sports league
item.description: Del Mar Middle School teams are playing the first season of a new countywide league, and its flag football program has grown from one coed team to two boys teams.
item.content:encoded:
Del Mar Middle School teams are playing the first season of a new countywide league, and its flag football program has grown from one coed team to two boys teams.

Del Mar Middle School’s teams are playing the first season of a countywide league run by the Marin County Office of Education, and the school’s flag football program has grown from one coed team to two boys teams.

The Marin Middle School Athletic League began competition Sept. 21 and includes 17 public middle schools and several private schools, according to the county education office. The league runs six sports: cross-country, flag football, volleyball, basketball, soccer, and track and field.

Although most of the sports were already offered through informal arrangements among Marin schools, the new league centralizes scheduling, rules, scores and officiating. Del Mar Athletic Director Jason Silva said that structure reduces the administrative burden previously carried by athletic directors and coaches.

item.title: Tiburon mahjong shop deals in tiles, lessons, community
item.description: San Rafael friends Maureen Riley and Daria Lovette opened California Mahjong House on Tiburon’s Ark Row, selling tiles and offering open play and lessons.
item.content:encoded:
San Rafael friends Maureen Riley and Daria Lovette opened California Mahjong House on Tiburon’s Ark Row, selling tiles and offering open play and lessons.

Like many in their circle, longtime friends Maureen “Moe” Riley and Daria Lovette got caught up in the nationwide mahjong revival about a year ago.

The two San Rafael residents each began having mahjong teachers to their homes after a friend asked whether they were interested in learning to play.

By May, in the middle of a game, they realized they wanted a dedicated space where they could touch and feel tiles and build community.

Their store, California Mahjong House, opened Aug. 26 on Ark Row. It sells tiles, mats, racks, bags and accessories such as hats and cocktail napkins, and players can join open play or take lessons at its eight tables.

item.title: A couple celebrates 25 years together with a Tiburon getaway
item.description: Campbell residents Sergio Herrera and Shannon Ives, married 25 years, came to Tiburon Oct. 27 to mark Ives’ 50th birthday with dinner at Malibu Farm.
item.content:encoded:
Campbell residents Sergio Herrera and Shannon Ives, married 25 years, came to Tiburon Oct. 27 to mark Ives’ 50th birthday with dinner at Malibu Farm.

Whenever Sergio Herrera and Shannon Ives are looking for a quick getaway, Tiburon is at the top of their destination list.

Married for 25 years, the Campbell residents were in town Oct. 27 to mark a milestone and stopped to watch construction near Fountain Plaza. Ives turned 50 the day before, and they celebrated with dinner at Malibu Farm.

“There was everything we could have expected it to be,” says Herrera, who ordered a pork chop while Ives had a pizza and the two shared cocktails.

item.title: Tiburon painter pairs abstracts with realistic scenes in Town Hall show
item.description: Tiburon painter Graciela Placak’s “Gracielaism” pairs abstract and realistic paintings at Tiburon Town Hall through Dec. 22, with a reception Nov. 10.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon painter Graciela Placak’s “Gracielaism” pairs abstract and realistic paintings at Tiburon Town Hall through Dec. 22, with a reception Nov. 10.

As much as Graciela Placak loves to paint, she refuses to do one kind of it: plein air painting. The first time Placak ventured outdoors to paint, she tripped and broke a toe. The second time, she set up her easel at Shoreline Park on Opening Day on the Bay. The weather was warm and sunny, and the painting was going well until the lawn sprinklers came on. Both she and her oil painting were soaked before she could get out of range. She says she won’t try a third time.

Despite her aversion to plein air, Placak, 64, says she was born to paint. Raised in Colombia in a family crowded with exceptional artists, she was encouraged to hone her creative skills.

That studio is now overflowing with works for her exhibit upstairs at Tiburon Town Hall. The show, titled “Gracielaism,” runs today, Nov. 4, through Dec. 22, with an artist reception from 6 to 8 p.m. Nov. 10.
item.dc:creator: Diane Smith
item.media:description: Tiburon artist Graciela Placak’s exhibit ‘Gracielaism’ runs through Dec. 22 upstairs at Tiburon Town Hall. (Bob Placak)

item.title: Cinelounge hosts Bruce Dern gala; Diwali festival is Saturday
item.description: Cinelounge Tiburon hosts Bruce Dern for a gala screening Nov. 5, and Tiburon’s fifth annual Diwali celebration runs 1-4 p.m. Nov. 7 at Zelinsky Park.
item.content:encoded:
Cinelounge Tiburon hosts Bruce Dern for a gala screening Nov. 5, and Tiburon’s fifth annual Diwali celebration runs 1-4 p.m. Nov. 7 at Zelinsky Park.

Cinelounge gala hosts Bruce Dern and documentary: Cinelounge Tiburon will host the first gala for its nonprofit, the Tiburon Playhouse Foundation, Nov. 5, screening “Dernsie: The Amazing Life of Bruce Dern” with the documentary’s subject in attendance. The evening starts at 5:30 p.m. with a reception for the actor, who has more than 200 film and TV credits going back to 1960. They include cult classics like “Silent Running” and “The ’Burbs,” along with “Black Sunday,” “The Great Gatsby,” “The Hateful Eight,” “The Driver” and Alfred Hitchcock’s final film, “Family Plot.” He earned two Oscar nominations 35 years apart, for “Coming Home” and “Nebraska.” Tickets are $70-$300. 415-797-6976 or cineloungefilm.com.

Diwali festival brings lights, music Saturday: Bollywood and bhangra dancing, live music and food vendors are on the program for Tiburon’s fifth annual Diwali celebration, set for 1-4 p.m. Nov. 7 at Zelinsky Park. The free event, sponsored by the town’s Diversity Inclusion Task Force, will feature a performance by Reed Elementary School students, a roaming dhol player and music from DJ Dev of Suhane Pal Music. The dhol is a barrel-shaped, double-headed drum. Diwali is observed by Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and some Buddhists in South Asia and across the diaspora. The five-day festival of lights honors the triumph of good over evil, knowledge over ignorance and light over darkness.
item.dc:creator: Diana Goodman

item.title: Lawrence H. Stotter
item.description: Lawrence H. Stotter (“Larry”) passed away peacefully at his home on October 25, 2026, at the age of 97. He is survived by his wife, Ruth Stotter; his children, Daniel Stotter, Jennifer Koran, and Steven Stotter; and his grandchildren, Benjamin Burress-Irving and Mia Koran. Born in Cleveland, Ohio, Larry was a graduate of Ohio State University College of Law, and was a nationally renowned family law attorney. He served as chair of the American Bar Association Section of Family Law, and was...
item.content:encoded:
Lawrence H. Stotter (“Larry”) passed away peacefully at his home on October 25, 2026, at the age of 97. He is survived by his wife, Ruth Stotter; his children, Daniel Stotter, Jennifer Koran, and Steven Stotter; and his grandchildren, Benjamin Burress-Irving and Mia Koran.

Born in Cleveland, Ohio, Larry was a graduate of Ohio State University College of Law, and was a nationally renowned family law attorney. He served as chair of the American Bar Association Section of Family Law, and was the U.S. delegate to the Hague Convention on International Child Abduction. Among his professional achievements, Larry won a landmark case before the U.S. Supreme Court involving interstate child custody. His research into the field of family law led to the publication of his 2011 book, “To Put Asunder: The Laws of Matrimonial Strife,” which traces over 2,000 years of family law history.

Larry served as chair of the Mount Tamalpais Conservation Club, reflecting his lifelong commitment to the conservation of the Bay Area’s natural environment, and he was a longtime volunteer with the Angel Island State Park. An avid reader, Larry also volunteered for the Friends of the Belvedere-Tiburon Library Bookstore. In the later years of his life, Larry became an accomplished masters track and field athlete, setting triple jump and sprint relay records in the 85+ age category. In 2016, at age 85, he was No. 1 nationally in the decathlon for his age group. He was also an active member of the Oakland, Mission Hills, and Sonoma-Cutrer croquet clubs.

Larry led a long and active life, devoted to his family, while pursuing professional excellence, conservation advocacy, athletic activities, and community service. He will be remembered by all whose lives he touched. Details on his celebration of life event will be shared when available.
item.dc:creator: Reader submitted

item.title: Tiburon, Belvedere brace for El Niño, king tides
item.description: Tiburon and Belvedere are filling sandbag stations and readying a shared emergency center for a strong to very strong El Niño, and officials urge residents to prepare.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon and Belvedere are filling sandbag stations and readying a shared emergency center for a strong to very strong El Niño, and officials urge residents to prepare.

Tiburon and Belvedere are filling sandbag stations and readying a shared emergency operations center for a winter that forecasters expect to bring a strong to very strong El Niño, and officials say residents need to get ready too.

NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center said Oct. 8 there is a “greater than an 83% chance” a strong to very strong El Niño lasts through January-March. It put the same 83% odds on October-December bringing an event stronger than any El Niño since 1950. Its next update is due Nov. 12.

NOAA’s Oct. 15 seasonal outlook gives much of California, and the West Coast as far north as the Oregon coast, elevated odds of above-normal rain from November through January, though with less confidence than for the Southeast.

The season’s highest tides are predicted Nov. 24-26, Dec. 22-25 and Jan. 20-22, topping out at 7.23 feet above the average daily low tide Dec. 24 at NOAA’s San Francisco gauge. Those predictions don’t account for weather, and actual tides have been running 6 inches to 1 foot higher, Steven Torrence, director of the county Office of Emergency Management, told the Belvedere-Tiburon Emergency Preparedness Council Oct. 20.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: A vehicle sits stranded on fully submerged Greenwood Cove Drive, left, while another works its way through the flooded inbound lanes of Tiburon Boulevard during the peak of the Jan. 3 king tide. Officials are preparing for a winter in which forecasters favor above-normal rain during a strong El Niño, with king tides expected Nov. 24-26, Dec. 22-25 and Jan. 20-22. item.title: Tiburon, Belvedere, Strawberry voters are weighing eight local contests, four local measures
item.description: Five candidates for three Tiburon Town Council seats and four for three Reed Union board seats head the peninsula’s Nov. 3 ballot, with six other races and four measures.
item.content:encoded:
Five candidates for three Tiburon Town Council seats and four for three Reed Union board seats head the peninsula’s Nov. 3 ballot, with six other races and four measures.

Five candidates for three Tiburon Town Council seats and four for three Reed Union School District board seats head the peninsula’s Nov. 3 local ballot, which also carries six other contested races and four local measures, including Reed Union’s $115 million bond.

Marin County elections officials began mailing ballots Oct. 5, and in-person voting is underway at the Marin County Civic Center. A vote center and an exterior drop box open Oct. 31 at Westminster Presbyterian Church in Tiburon, and the 24-hour drop box at Belvedere City Hall is already open. Both drop boxes close at 8 p.m. Election Day, Nov. 3, when every vote center is open 7 a.m.-8 p.m.

Not every race is on every ballot, and each section notes which voters decide it. The Ark’s full stories on most of these races and measures are at thearknewspaper.com/election2026. The state and federal contests ran in the Oct. 7 edition.

Town council, Tiburon voters

Mayor Jon Welner isn’t seeking reelection, so at least one newcomer will join the council. Councilmember Alice Fredericks, on the council since 2001 and a five-time mayor, is seeking a seventh term. Councilmember Jack Ryan, a retired derivatives trading manager first elected in a 2020 special election and mayor in 2023, is seeking a second full term. The challengers are Planning Commissioner Kathleen Defever, an attorney who lost council bids in 2020 and 2021; Chuck Hornbrook, a member of the Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission who ran fourth in 2024; and Faris Jafar, founder of the wealth-management firm Jafar Management and a member of the Reed district’s budget advisory committee.

item.title: Nine-townhome plan for Point Tiburon clears key hurdle after three rejections
item.description: Tiburon deemed Black Oak Ventures’ fourth application for nine townhomes on the Point Tiburon Plaza parking lot complete Oct. 22; the town must decide by Nov. 23.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon deemed Black Oak Ventures’ fourth application for nine townhomes on the Point Tiburon Plaza parking lot complete Oct. 22; the town must decide by Nov. 23.

After three failed submissions over the past year, a Berkeley developer has cleared a major hurdle to build nine townhomes on part of the Point Tiburon Plaza parking lot.

Tiburon notified Black Oak Ventures Oct. 22 that the fourth version of its 1801 Tiburon Blvd. application is complete. The town now has until Nov. 23, 60 days after Black Oak filed that version Sept. 24, to approve or deny the project, Tiburon Senior Planner Kristin Teiche has said.

“We are pleased that the town has confirmed that our application is complete and look forward to receiving the approval of the application within weeks,” Black Oak founder and principal owner Michael Yarne said Oct. 23.

Yarne’s firm is working with Point Tiburon Plaza owner Chong Cook to subdivide part of the parking lot into nine lots for detached three-story townhomes, each with a two-car garage and partial storage cellar.

item.title: Tiburon sailor’s America’s Cup campaign reaches the big screen
item.description: “Mighty Mary,” a new documentary about the 1995 all-women America’s Cup crew, recounts the campaign of Tiburon’s Melissa Purdy Feagin, the boat’s mainsail trimmer.
item.content:encoded:
“Mighty Mary,” a new documentary about the 1995 all-women America’s Cup crew, recounts the campaign of Tiburon’s Melissa Purdy Feagin, the boat’s mainsail trimmer.

More than three decades after Tiburon resident Melissa Purdy Feagin helped propel the first all-woman America’s Cup team through one of the world’s most prestigious competitions, she is watching the story of Mighty Mary reach a new audience.

“Mighty Mary,” a new feature-length documentary, recounts the 1995 campaign in which the crew competed for the right to defend the America’s Cup. Feagin, then Melissa Purdy, was the boat’s mainsail trimmer, controlling the sail’s shape and tension to help keep the 55,000-pound yacht moving at top speed.

The 98-minute documentary, directed by former Olympic rower Mary Mazzio and narrated by actors Hugh Jackman and Elizabeth Banks, opened in select theaters nationwide Sept. 11. It screens at 8 p.m. Nov. 4 and 5 at the Marina Theatre on Chestnut Street in San Francisco, where both showings are scheduled to include Q&A sessions with members of the film’s cast. Feagin plans to attend the Nov. 5 screening.

The film revisits a campaign in which Mighty Mary took on teams led by some of the most experienced sailors in America’s Cup history and nearly advanced to defend the trophy before a series of internal conflicts, personnel changes and competition decisions altered its course.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Melissa Purdy Feagin of Tiburon wears an America3 team vest during the 1995 America’s Cup campaign, when she trimmed the mainsail for the Mighty Mary crew, the first all-women team to contend for the cup. (via Melissa Purdy Feagin)

item.title: Reed Union schools to develop age-based framework for screens, AI
item.description: Reed Union School District board members questioned student screen time Oct. 13; a framework setting age-appropriate limits on devices and AI comes to the board in February.
item.content:encoded:
Reed Union School District board members questioned student screen time Oct. 13; a framework setting age-appropriate limits on devices and AI comes to the board in February.

Four months after approving the district’s first artificial intelligence policy, Reed Union School District board members used their first look at a districtwide technology plan to ask whether students from preschool through eighth grade spend too long on screens.

Jonathan Weller, the district’s director of information systems, educational technology and innovation, told the board Oct. 13 that a framework setting age-appropriate limits on devices and AI will come to the board in February.

Board members’ concerns surfaced minutes earlier, during an update on curriculum pilots, when board member Mike Ghaffary said classrooms should use real textbooks and paper and pencil whenever possible.

“I think the whole world has jumped the shark on overreliance on technology,” Ghaffary said.

item.title: Late filings show who’s paying for Tiburon council, fire, school races
item.description: Alice Fredericks raised the most from donors among Tiburon Town Council candidates in the last pre-election reports, while Kathleen Defever outspent the field with a loan.
item.content:encoded:
Alice Fredericks raised the most from donors among Tiburon Town Council candidates in the last pre-election reports, while Kathleen Defever outspent the field with a loan.

Incumbent Councilmember Alice Fredericks raised the most money from donors among Tiburon’s Town Council candidates in the last campaign-finance reports before the Nov. 3 election, while challenger Kathleen Defever outspent the field with money she lent her own campaign.

Fredericks reported $2,124 in monetary contributions in the period from Sept. 20 to Oct. 17, the last preelection disclosure ahead of the Nov. 3 race for three seats. She reported spending $4,457 in the period.

Planning Commissioner Defever reported the largest total, $10,850, but $9,400 of it is a loan she made to her own campaign. The other $1,450 came from donors.

Keep election coverage free

The Ark doesn’t put its election coverage behind a paywall, so every voter in Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry can read it. A gift keeps it that way.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Parks, Open Space & Trails Commissioner Chuck Hornbrook reported $1,662 in contributions, $1,350 of it from donors, and investment-fund founder Faris Jafar reported $1,591 in donations.

Defever also reported the most spending in the period, $8,462. Hornbrook reported $4,828 in expenditures, Fredericks $4,457 and Jafar $3,453.

The California Fair Political Practices Commission requires two campaign-finance disclosures before an election from candidates who raise or spend $2,000 or more. The first, due Sept. 24, covered July 1-Sept. 19.

The other incumbent seeking reelection, Councilmember Jack Ryan, did not need to submit a campaign-finance report, as he filed a statement Sept. 16 saying he expects to receive and spend less than $2,000 this year.

Elsewhere on peninsula ballots, firefighter unions put money behind two Southern Marin Fire Protection District challengers, and a new committee reported spending against Marin County Board of Education incumbent Marilyn Nemzer.

Defever received $500 each from Tiburon resident Hank McWhinney and part-time Strawberry resident Priya Clemens, $250 from Tiburon attorney Jon Rankin and $100 each from Tiburon residents John B. Snell and Belle Guelden. She lent her campaign the $9,400 on Oct. 4 and another $5,600 on Oct. 23, according to 24-hour reports she filed Oct. 22 and Oct. 26.

item.title: Developer agrees to pay Strawberry neighbors $100,000 to end senior-housing suit
item.description: Spirit Living Group will pay Tiburon Ridge Neighbors $100,000 to end their suit over its shelved Strawberry senior-housing complex; it remains free to apply again.
item.content:encoded:
Spirit Living Group will pay Tiburon Ridge Neighbors $100,000 to end their suit over its shelved Strawberry senior-housing complex; it remains free to apply again.

The developer of a shelved senior-housing complex on a Strawberry hillside has agreed to pay neighbors who sued over it $100,000 to end the case, under a settlement that leaves the company free to apply again and the neighbors free to challenge it.

Spirit Living Group agreed to pay the 60-member Tiburon Ridge Neighbors and its leader, Scott Arwin, $100,000 for legal expenses and costs, according to a copy of the settlement agreement Marin County Counsel Brandon Halter provided to The Ark Oct. 19. Apart from that payment, each party covers its own attorney fees and costs.

The county, whose December approval the neighbors challenged, is a party to the settlement but paid nothing, Halter said.

But the deal covers only the county’s Dec. 23 approval, which the county voided in June at the developer’s request. It “does not bar any challenge to any future application” for the 100 Thomas Place parcels, and it does not bind any party on a future project at the same site. No party admits liability.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Octogenarian Marin rowing crew with Tiburon’s Kim Coggan takes on Head of the Charles
item.description: Tiburon’s Kim Coggan and her Marin Rowing Association crew, average age 80, raced the Head of the Charles in Boston Oct. 17, finishing nearly three minutes faster than expected.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon’s Kim Coggan and her Marin Rowing Association crew, average age 80, raced the Head of the Charles in Boston Oct. 17, finishing nearly three minutes faster than expected.

At 77, Tiburon resident Kim Coggan cannot power a racing shell the way she once did. Her crew’s stroke rate has slowed, and recovery requires more attention. But on Oct. 17 on the Charles River in Boston, Coggan and seven longtime teammates raced the course in a little more than 27 minutes, nearly three minutes faster than they had expected.

The Marin Rowing Association crew, which club members say was the first women’s eight with an average age of 80 to race the Head of the Charles Regatta, finished in 27 minutes, 6 seconds, in the regatta’s women’s veteran eights.

The crew finished last of 25 in a field made up mostly of crews in their 60s, the only boat in the 80-and-older category.

“We knew that what we had to do was recognize our strengths,” Coggan said. “We don’t have the power that younger crews do, but we can row well together.”
